items.title: Top 5 Tallest Mountains in the Solar System (Everest Doesn't Make It) #shorts
items.description:
From Hawaii to Mars: the five tallest mountains we know, measured base to summit, with Everest for scale.
Full video: What If Earth Had Rings Like Saturn? It May Have Had One 466 Million Years Ago

Sources
• USGS / NOAA: Mauna Kea rises about 4,207 m above sea level and more than 10,000 m from its base on the sea floor
• Schenk et al. (2001), Journal of Geophysical Research (Voyager and Galileo data): Boösaule Montes on Io about 17.5 km high, a tectonic mountain
• NASA / Cassini: Iapetus's equatorial ridge rises up to about 20 km
• NASA / Dawn: the central peak of Vesta's Rheasilvia crater rises about 22 km; some measurements put it close to Olympus Mons
• NASA: Olympus Mons on Mars is about 25 km high, almost three times Mount Everest, and about the size of Arizona
• Nepal and China (2020): Mount Everest 8,849 m above sea level
• Own calculation: 25 / 8.849 ≈ 2.8 Everests

Visuals are original. Narration uses a synthetic voice.
#shorts #space #mars #science

items.title: What If Earth Had Rings Like Saturn? It May Have Had One 466 Million Years Ago
items.description:
Give Earth rings like Saturn's and the view changes with every city: a thin line over Quito, a giant arch over Mexico City, only the outer rings from London, and nothing at all from Reykjavik. Then the fine print: brighter nights, darker winters under the ring shadow, satellites forced around a no-fly zone, and rings that slowly rain away. And the twist: Earth may have really had a ring about 466 million years ago.

Chapters
0:00 What you'd see from New York
0:35 Building Saturn's rings around Earth
1:17 Only 10 meters thick
1:55 Postcard 1: Quito, on the equator
2:26 Postcard 2: Mexico City
2:57 Postcard 3: New York
3:13 Postcard 4: London
3:26 Postcard 5: Reykjavik
4:11 Brighter nights
4:28 Darker winters: the ring shadow
5:14 Satellites vs rings
5:38 Rings don't last: ring rain
6:12 Twist: did Earth already have a ring?
7:10 Mars will get a ring
7:29 Recap and next episode

Sources
• NASA Science, Saturn's rings: main rings extend up to about 282,000 km from the planet but are about 10 m thick in most places; made mostly of water ice, from tiny grains to large chunks
• NASA Saturnian Rings Fact Sheet: ring radii (C ring 74,658–92,000 km, B ring 92,000–117,580 km, Cassini Division 117,580–122,170 km, A ring 122,170–136,775 km); Saturn's equatorial radius 60,268 km
• NASA / O'Donoghue et al. (2018), Icarus: 'ring rain' drains about an Olympic pool of material every half hour; rings could be gone in about 300 million years, possibly under 100 million with Cassini data
• Iess et al. (2019), Science (Cassini Grand Finale): low ring mass, consistent with relatively young rings
• Tomkins, Martin & Cawood (2024), Earth and Planetary Science Letters, 'Evidence suggesting that Earth had a ring in the Ordovician': 21 impact craters from about 466 million years ago, all within 30° of the equator; proposed ring and possible link to the Hirnantian icehouse
• Eos (AGU), 2024: other researchers call for more precise crater dating before accepting the ring hypothesis
• Black & Mittal (2015), Nature Geoscience, 'The demise of Phobos and development of a Martian ring system': Phobos breaks into a ring in about 20 to 40 million years
• NASA: International Space Station orbits about 400–420 km up; GPS satellites about 20,200 km; geostationary orbit 35,786 km
• Own calculations (Python): Saturn's rings scaled to Earth = 7,900–14,500 km from the centre (1,500–8,100 km up); ring edges visible from the ground only where cos(latitude) is greater than 1/r (inner ring up to about 36°, outer edge up to about 64°); noon ring shadow on the winter solstice for 23.44° axial tilt (B ring about 14°–27°, whole ring system about 7°–41°); Roche limit 2.44 R (density ratio)^(1/3) about 28,400 km for ice and 19,000 km for rock; 273,000 km / 10 m = 27 million, so paper-thin rings would be about 2.7 km wide

—
Cosmic Scale: the universe, measured in a way you can feel.

Visuals and animations are original. Narration uses a synthetic voice.

items.title: Saturn's Rings Are Thinner Than a Building (and 273,000 km Wide) #shorts
items.description:
273,000 km across, about 10 meters thick. Saturn's rings, measured in a way you can feel.
Full video: What If Earth Had Rings Like Saturn? It May Have Had One 466 Million Years Ago

Sources
• NASA Science, Saturn's rings: the main rings span about 273,000 km and are about 10 m thick in most places
• NASA Saturnian Rings Fact Sheet: A ring outer edge 136,775 km from Saturn's centre
• NASA (2025): Saturn's rings appeared edge-on from Earth in March 2025 (ring-plane crossing) and nearly disappeared in telescopes
• Own calculations: 273,550 km / 384,400 km ≈ 0.71 of the Earth–Moon distance; 273,000 km / 10 m = 27 million, so paper-thin (0.1 mm) rings would be about 2.7 km wide

Visuals are original. Narration uses a synthetic voice.
#shorts #space #saturn #science
